llm: Large Language Model: an AI model trained on huge amounts of text to generate and understand language.
transformer: The neural network architecture behind most modern language models, built around the attention mechanism.
attention mechanism: A technique that lets a model weigh how much each part of the input matters when producing an output.
fine-tuning: Further training a pretrained model on a smaller, specific dataset to specialize it for a task.
pretraining: The initial, large-scale training phase where a model learns general patterns from broad data before any specialization.
rlhf: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: training a model using human preference ratings to steer its behavior.
rag: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: having a model look up relevant documents before answering, instead of relying only on what it memorized.
embedding: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, image, or other data so it can be compared mathematically.
token: A chunk of text (often a word piece) that a language model reads or generates one at a time.
tokenizer: The component that splits raw text into tokens a model can process.
inference: Running a trained model to produce an output, as opposed to training it.
quantization: Shrinking a model by using lower-precision numbers to store its weights, trading a little accuracy for speed and smaller size.
lora: Low-Rank Adaptation: a lightweight way to fine-tune a model by training a small set of extra parameters instead of the whole model.
parameter: A learned number inside a model that gets adjusted during training; "billions of parameters" describes model size.
weights: Another name for a model's learned parameters.
checkpoint: A saved snapshot of a model's weights at a point in training.
benchmark: A standardized test used to measure and compare model performance.
hallucination: When a model confidently states something false or made up.
context window: The maximum amount of text a model can consider at once when generating a response.
latency: How long a model takes to respond after receiving a request.
throughput: How many requests or tokens a system can process in a given amount of time.
gpu: Graphics Processing Unit: specialized hardware that makes the parallel math behind AI training and inference fast.
vram: The memory on a GPU, which limits how large a model you can run on it.
distillation: Training a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher" model, keeping much of its capability at lower cost.
reward model: A model trained to score how good an output is, used to guide another model's training.
reasoning model: A model trained or prompted to work through intermediate steps before giving a final answer.
chain of thought: Prompting or training a model to write out its intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer.
multimodal: Able to work with more than one type of data, such as text, images, or audio, at once.
vision-language model: A model that can process both images and text together.
diffusion model: A generative model that creates data (often images) by gradually turning noise into a coherent output.
gan: Generative Adversarial Network: a setup where two models compete, one generating fake data and one trying to detect it, improving both.
autoregressive: Generating output one piece at a time, where each new piece depends on the ones before it.
zero-shot: Getting a model to perform a task it was never explicitly trained or shown examples for.
few-shot: Giving a model a handful of examples in the prompt to guide it on a new task.
prompt engineering: Crafting the wording and structure of an input to get better output from a model.
system prompt: Instructions given to a model ahead of a conversation to set its behavior or persona.
agent: A system that uses a model to take actions, like calling tools or browsing, toward a goal rather than just generating text.
function calling: A model's ability to call external functions or APIs as part of producing its answer.
vector database: A database optimized for storing and searching embeddings by similarity.
open weights: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, as opposed to only being accessible via an API.
open source: Software, or loosely a model, released with its underlying code or weights and a license allowing reuse and modification.
api: Application Programming Interface: a defined way for one piece of software to request functionality from another, such as calling a hosted model.
dataset: The collection of examples used to train or evaluate a model.
overfitting: When a model learns its training data too specifically and performs worse on new, unseen data.
generalization: A model's ability to perform well on data it wasn't directly trained on.
gradient descent: The core optimization method used to train neural networks by nudging their parameters to reduce error.
loss function: A formula that measures how wrong a model's predictions are, which training tries to minimize.
batch size: The number of training examples processed together before a model's parameters are updated once.
epoch: One full pass through the entire training dataset.
synthetic data: Artificially generated data, often produced by another model, used to train or augment a dataset.
mixture of experts: A model architecture that routes each input to a subset of specialized "expert" sub-networks instead of using the whole model every time.
instruction tuning: Fine-tuning a model on examples of instructions and desired responses so it follows commands better.
alignment: Techniques aimed at making a model's behavior match human intentions and values.
